pos: n. (Aramaic; the fourth word of the writing on Belshazzar's wall)
etymology: Aramaic u-pharsin, and they divide, the conjunction u prefixed to the plural of peras, to divide or to break in two; left untranslated by the Authorized Version at Daniel 5:25.
biblical_def: Upharsin is the fourth and last word of the writing that a hand wrote on the plaster of Belshazzar's banqueting hall: “And this is the writing that was written, MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN” (Daniel 5:25). The Authorized Version leaves all four words standing in their own tongue, and then lets Daniel translate them one at a time. Mene is numbering: “MENE; God hath numbered thy kingdom, and finished it” (Daniel 5:26). Tekel is weighing: “TEKEL; Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting” (Daniel 5:27). And Upharsin is dividing, which Daniel gives in the singular form Peres: “PERES; Thy kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians” (Daniel 5:28). The u at the front is simply the Aramaic and, so the word reads and they divide. There is a sharpness in the word Daniel chose: peres for dividing sounds in Aramaic like Paras, Persia. The sentence names the sin and the executioner in one breath. Belshazzar was counted, weighed and cut up, and the kingdom he had drunk to was handed over before the night was done.

corruption_summary: Nations assume that power once held is power retained; Upharsin is the word for a kingdom cut in pieces in a night.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern state reckons its continuance a matter of economics and arms, and the modern man reckons his own the same way. The writing on the wall says that a kingdom is numbered, weighed and divided by a God who keeps the accounts, and that the sentence may be executed the same evening it is read.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God numbers, weighs and divides the kingdoms of men, and that no feast, however loud, delays the reckoning by an hour.

pos: n. (Hebrew; a password at the fords of Jordan, used as a test of speech)
etymology: Hebrew shibboleth, an ear of corn, or a flowing stream; left untranslated by the Authorized Version at Judges 12:6, where it serves as a test word.
biblical_def: Shibboleth is the Hebrew word the men of Gilead set as a test at the fords of Jordan after Jephthah's war with Ephraim. The quarrel began in wounded pride: “And the men of Ephraim gathered themselves together, and went northward, and said unto Jephthah, Wherefore passedst thou over to fight against the children of Ammon, and didst not call us to go with thee?” (Judges 12:1). It ended in slaughter, and the slaughter was sifted by a syllable. “And the Gileadites took the passages of Jordan before the Ephraimites” (Judges 12:5), and every man who claimed not to be an Ephraimite was handed the word: “Then said they unto him, Say now Shibboleth: and he said Sibboleth: for he could not frame to pronounce it right. Then they took him, and slew him at the passages of Jordan: and there fell at that time of the Ephraimites forty and two thousand” (Judges 12:6). The word itself means an ear of corn, or a flood of water; the meaning was nothing, the sound was everything. Ephraim could not make the sh. From this passage English has taken the word shibboleth for any token of party that distinguishes insiders from outsiders without testing anything of substance.

The Ephraimites could not frame to pronounce it rightly, and were slain.

corruption_summary: A party badge is mistaken for a confession; Gilead killed by accent what it could not try by faith.
corruption_paragraphs: Churches and movements still set shibboleths: a phrase, a translation, a style of dress, a stance on a disputed thing of no weight, by which a man is counted friend or enemy before anyone asks what he believes. The test at Jordan was merciless precisely because it was shallow, and brothers died over a consonant.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the church tries men by confession and conduct, not by accent or faction, and that a civil war between brethren is a judgment before it is a victory.

pos: n. (Hebrew; a stringed instrument, named in the title of the sixty-first psalm)
etymology: Hebrew neginah, the music of a stringed instrument, from nagan, to touch or play the strings; left untranslated by the Authorized Version in the title of Psalm 61.
biblical_def: Neginah is the Hebrew term the Authorized Version leaves standing in the superscription of the sixty-first psalm: “To the chief Musician upon Neginah, A Psalm of David. Hear my cry, O God; attend unto my prayer” (Psalm 61:1). It denotes the music of a stringed instrument, from the verb nagan, to touch the strings, and it is the singular of the Neginoth that heads several other psalms. The direction is a plain fact about the worship of Israel: these were not private poems but appointed music, handed to a chief musician with instructions for the instrument. The psalm itself is the prayer of a man a long way from home and at the end of his strength: “From the end of the earth will I cry unto thee, when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to the rock that is higher than I” (Psalm 61:2). He pleads a tried history: “For thou hast been a shelter for me, and a strong tower from the enemy” (Psalm 61:3), and he asks for the one lodging he wants: “I will abide in thy tabernacle for ever: I will trust in the covert of thy wings” (Psalm 61:4). That such a cry was set to the strings and sung in the congregation tells us what Israel's public worship was willing to say out loud.

corruption_paragraphs: It is now usual to treat the psalm superscriptions as editorial scraps of no authority, which conveniently removes both their authorship notes and their musical directions. The Authorized Version prints them as text. They tell us that the songs of Israel were composed by named men, delivered to a chief musician, and set to appointed instruments — worship ordered rather than improvised.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that public worship is appointed and instructed, and that the most overwhelmed cry a believer has may be set to music and sung in the congregation.

pos: n. (Hebrew; a musical or poetic direction in the title of Habakkuk's prayer)
etymology: Hebrew shigyonoth, plural of shiggaion, perhaps a wandering or impassioned song, from shagah, to wander or reel; left untranslated by the Authorized Version at Habakkuk 3:1.
biblical_def: Shigionoth is the Hebrew direction the Authorized Version leaves untranslated over the third chapter of Habakkuk: “A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet upon Shigionoth” (Habakkuk 3:1). It is the plural of shiggaion, the word that heads the seventh psalm, and it is thought to mark an impassioned or wandering song — a piece carried by strong feeling rather than measured calm. Whatever the precise musical sense, the chapter it introduces is exactly that. The prophet has been told that Babylon is coming, and he answers with dread and with intercession in the same verse: “O LORD, I have heard thy speech, and was afraid: O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years, in the midst of the years make known; in wrath remember mercy” (Habakkuk 3:2). Then comes a vision of God marching through the land, and at the end the famous turn in which a man with no harvest left declares his joy: “Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation” (Habakkuk 3:18). The chapter closes as a psalm closes, with the instrument named: “The LORD God is my strength, and he will make my feet like hinds' feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places” (Habakkuk 3:19). A prophet's terror was set to music and sung.

corruption_summary: Strong feeling in worship is set against sound doctrine; Shigionoth heads a chapter in which a trembling prophet sings true theology.
corruption_paragraphs: Worship is commonly forced to choose between heat and light — either passion without doctrine or doctrine without passion. Habakkuk's prayer upon Shigionoth is a trembling, impassioned song, and it is also one of the most exact accounts of divine judgment and mercy in the prophets. The fear and the theology are the same breath.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a believer may rejoice in the God of his salvation when the fig tree does not blossom, and that such rejoicing is a reasoned act, not a mood.

pos: n. (Hebrew; part of the musical direction in the title of the eighty-eighth psalm)
etymology: Hebrew le-'annoth, for afflicting or to humble, from anah, to afflict or bow down; left untranslated by the Authorized Version in the title of Psalm 88, where it follows Mahalath.
biblical_def: Leannoth is the second half of the musical direction the Authorized Version leaves standing over the eighty-eighth psalm: “A Song or Psalm for the sons of Korah, to the chief Musician upon Mahalath Leannoth, Maschil of Heman the Ezrahite. O LORD God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee” (Psalm 88:1). Mahalath is sickness, and Leannoth comes from the Hebrew verb to afflict or to bow down, so the pair reads roughly concerning sickness, for afflicting — a tune or a manner of singing fitted to grief. The title is honest advertising. This is the darkest psalm in the Psalter. The singer asks only to be heard: “Let my prayer come before thee: incline thine ear unto my cry” (Psalm 88:2); he reports his condition plainly: “For my soul is full of troubles: and my life draweth nigh unto the grave” (Psalm 88:3); and he ends without relief: “Lover and friend hast thou put far from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness” (Psalm 88:18). That the congregation of Israel was given a song for affliction which does not resolve is a mercy. God made room in His own hymnbook for the believer who sees no morning yet.

corruption_summary: Grief is treated as a failure of faith; Leannoth labels an inspired song of affliction that never resolves.
corruption_paragraphs: Much modern worship has no room for a believer in the dark. A song must end in a lifted chorus, and a saint who cannot sing it is quietly judged. The eighty-eighth psalm was given to the chief musician with a direction for affliction, and it ends with acquaintance put into darkness. God does not require His people to lie about their condition before He will hear them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that lament is an appointed form of worship, that a psalm may end unresolved and still be inspired, and that crying day and night before God is faith and not its failure.

pos: n. (Hebrew; an article of the trade of Judah with Tyre, left untranslated)
etymology: Hebrew pannag, a commodity of uncertain kind, perhaps a sweet confection, a balm, or a kind of grain; left untranslated by the Authorized Version at Ezekiel 27:17.
biblical_def: Pannag is one of the few words in the Authorized Version that the translators declined to render because they did not know what it was. It stands in the inventory of Tyre's commerce, among the goods Judah sent down to the great market of the sea: “Judah, and the land of Israel, they were thy merchants: they traded in thy market wheat of Minnith, and Pannag, and honey, and oil, and balm” (Ezekiel 27:17). It sits between named grain and named sweetness, so it has been taken for a confection, a cake, a spice, or a kind of millet; the honest answer is that the word occurs once in Scripture and nowhere else in Hebrew, and its sense is lost. The chapter around it is a merchant's ledger turned into a funeral song. Syria traded in emeralds and fine linen, “they occupied in thy fairs with emeralds, purple, and broidered work, and fine linen, and coral, and agate” (Ezekiel 27:16); Damascus brought the wine of Helbon and white wool, “Damascus was thy merchant in the multitude of the wares of thy making” (Ezekiel 27:18). And the end of all that commerce is one line: “The merchants among the people shall hiss at thee; thou shalt be a terror, and never shalt be any more” (Ezekiel 27:36).

corruption_summary: Translators are faulted for admitting ignorance; Pannag stands untranslated because honesty was preferred to a guess.
corruption_paragraphs: A version is often praised for being smooth and blamed for being strange, and so a hard word gets a confident English equivalent it cannot bear. The men who gave us the Authorized Version left Pannag as they found it. That is not a defect in the translation; it is a mark of its conscience, and the reader is told plainly where the ground is uncertain.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that fidelity sometimes requires leaving a word alone, and that the wealth of nations, inventoried in detail, ends in a hiss when God rises against it.

pos: n. (the Egyptian name Pharaoh gave to Joseph)
etymology: Egyptian, given in Hebrew letters as Tsaphnath Pa'neach; the margin of the Authorized Version renders it a revealer of secrets, or the man to whom secrets are revealed.
biblical_def: Zaphnath-paaneah is the Egyptian name Pharaoh laid upon Joseph on the day he raised him over the land. The elevation is told in three strokes: “And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, See, I have set thee over all the land of Egypt” (Genesis 41:41); “And he made him to ride in the second chariot which he had; and they cried before him, Bow the knee: and he made him ruler over all the land of Egypt” (Genesis 41:43); and then the new name and the new wife: “And Pharaoh called Joseph's name Zaphnathpaaneah; and he gave him to wife Asenath the daughter of Potipherah priest of On” (Genesis 41:45). The name is Egyptian, not Hebrew, and the margin of the Authorized Version gives the old understanding of it as a revealer of secrets. Pharaoh had just confessed that the secret was not in Joseph but in Joseph's God, and the court nevertheless named the man for the gift. He was thirty years old: “And Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh king of Egypt” (Genesis 41:46) — the age at which another Son of promise would begin His ministry. A Hebrew slave bore an Egyptian name, married an Egyptian wife, and governed the house of his exile, and all of it served the keeping alive of a family he had not yet forgiven.

corruption_paragraphs: A man who is used of God is quickly renamed by the world for the usefulness: the revealer, the visionary, the one with the gift. Joseph had said plainly that interpretations belong to God, and he was promptly titled as though the secrets were his own. Every servant of God who is honored for his labors must keep hold of the distinction Pharaoh did not grasp.

pos: n. (the name Jeremiah gave to Pashur the priest)
etymology: Hebrew Magor missabib, terror round about or fear on every side, from magor, terror, and missabib, from round about; left untranslated by the Authorized Version at Jeremiah 20:3.
biblical_def: Magor-missabib is the name the prophet Jeremiah gave to Pashur the priest, who had struck him and shut him in the stocks. When the night of that humiliation was over, the prisoner named his jailer: “And it came to pass on the morrow, that Pashur brought forth Jeremiah out of the stocks. Then said Jeremiah unto him, The LORD hath not called thy name Pashur, but Magormissabib” (Jeremiah 20:3). The Hebrew means terror round about, and the sentence that follows explains it: “For thus saith the LORD, Behold, I will make thee a terror to thyself, and to all thy friends: and they shall fall by the sword of their enemies, and thine eyes shall behold it” (Jeremiah 20:4). The irony cuts both ways, for the same phrase, fear on every side, is what Jeremiah himself heard from his neighbours: “For I heard the defaming of many, fear on every side. Report, say they, and we will report it” (Jeremiah 20:10). The persecuted prophet and the persecuting priest were encircled by the same dread; the difference was who stood with them. “But the LORD is with me as a mighty terrible one: therefore my persecutors shall stumble, and they shall not prevail” (Jeremiah 20:11).

corruption_paragraphs: A man with a sacred title assumes the title protects him, and those under it often assume so too. Pashur held the office and used it to beat a prophet. God changed his name, which in Scripture is to change his standing, and the terror he had dealt out became the terror he lived in.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is not deceived by office, that persecutors of His word are renamed by their end, and that a faithful man encircled by fear is not thereby forsaken.

pos: n. (a rock in the wilderness of Maon where Saul turned back from David)
etymology: Hebrew Sela ha-machleqoth; the margin of the Authorized Version renders it the rock of divisions, from sela, a rock, and chalaq, to divide or separate.
biblical_def: Sela-hammahlekoth is the name given to a rock in the wilderness where Saul, within reach of David, was turned aside. The hunt had closed: “And Saul went on this side of the mountain, and David and his men on that side of the mountain: and David made haste to get away for fear of Saul; for Saul and his men compassed David and his men round about to take them” (1 Samuel 23:26). There was no escape on the ground; the escape came by news out of another country: “But there came a messenger unto Saul, saying, Haste thee, and come; for the Philistines have invaded the land” (1 Samuel 23:27). So the king broke off the pursuit: “Wherefore Saul returned from pursuing after David, and went against the Philistines: therefore they called that place Selahammahlekoth” (1 Samuel 23:28). The margin of the Authorized Version gives the sense as the rock of divisions — the rock where the two parties were divided. David went on to safer ground: “And David went up from thence, and dwelt in strong holds at Engedi” (1 Samuel 23:29). The place was named for a deliverance that no one in it arranged. God moved a Philistine army to save an anointed man He had promised to keep.

corruption_summary: Deliverance is credited to timing or luck; the rock of divisions was named for a rescue God arranged through an invading army.
corruption_paragraphs: Men call such an escape a close call, a coincidence, a lucky break in the weather of events. David's men named the rock. They understood that the Philistine invasion which pulled Saul away was not an accident of the calendar but the hand of God keeping a promise, and they left a name on the ground so no one would forget it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God governs the armies of the heathen for the keeping of His own, and that His people ought to mark the places of their deliverance.

pos: n. (a possession David took from the Philistines)
etymology: Hebrew Metheg ha-ammah; the margin of the Authorized Version renders it the bridle of Ammah, from metheg, a bridle, and ammah, a mother-city or a cubit.
biblical_def: Metheg-ammah is what David took out of the hand of the Philistines at the opening of the chapter that catalogues his victories: “And after this it came to pass, that David smote the Philistines, and subdued them: and David took Methegammah out of the hand of the Philistines” (2 Samuel 8:1). The Authorized Version leaves the word standing and gives in the margin the bridle of Ammah. Whether it names a city, a chief fortress, or the control of a district, the figure is a bridle — the thing by which Philistia had held the land, taken now into David's hand. What follows in the chapter shows the same hand at work: “And he smote Moab, and measured them with a line, casting them down to the ground; even with two lines measured he to put to death, and with one full line to keep alive” (2 Samuel 8:2); “Then David put garrisons in Syria of Damascus: and the Syrians became servants to David, and brought gifts” (2 Samuel 8:6); “And he put garrisons in Edom; throughout all Edom put he garrisons, and all they of Edom became David's servants” (2 Samuel 8:14). Twice in that chapter the historian stops the ledger of conquests to name the cause: the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went.

corruption_summary: Victory is read as competence; the chapter that lists David's conquests twice names the LORD as the preserver.
corruption_paragraphs: A run of success invites a man to study his own methods. Second Samuel eight is a plain military ledger — Philistia, Moab, Syria, Edom, garrisons, tribute, spoil — and twice the writer interrupts the accounting to say that the LORD preserved David wherever he went. The bridle came out of Philistine hands into David's because God put it there.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD gives victory and preserves His servant, and that the record of a man's successes is rightly read as a record of God's keeping.
